simple: many computers that look, to their users and programs, like one computer.
analogy: four friends' rooms that callers experience as one clubhouse.
precise: the property of a distributed system that presents one set of names, processes, files and devices, so that users and programs need not know which machine holds what; the degree to which this holds is described by the transparencies it provides.
source: D1 of F5-44 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): introduction (goals, distribution transparency and its limits, t) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: hiding a fact about the many machines from the user.
analogy: the caller does not hear which friend's shelf the book came from.
precise: hiding a property of distribution: access (local and remote use look the same), location (names do not say where), migration and relocation (things may move), replication (copies look like one), concurrency (sharing looks private), failure (crashes are masked). Full transparency is neither always possible nor always wise.
source: D1 of F5-44 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): introduction (goals, distribution transparency and its limits, t) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one operating system spread over many machines.
analogy: one club rulebook that every friend follows in the same way.
precise: an operating system whose kernels on all machines cooperate to manage the machines' resources as one system, usually with one name space and one process model; contrasted with a network operating system and with middleware.
source: D1 of F5-44 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): introduction (goals, distribution transparency and its limits, t) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: separate computers, each with its own operating system, that can use each other's services.
analogy: four separate clubs that lend each other books on request.
precise: independent operating systems on each machine, joined by services such as remote login and remote files that the user invokes explicitly; each machine keeps its own names and processes.
source: D1 of F5-44 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): introduction (goals, distribution transparency and its limits, t) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a software layer above ordinary operating systems that makes many machines easier to use together.
analogy: a shared club notebook kept on top of four separate homes.
precise: a layer between applications and the (network) operating systems that provides distribution services such as remote calls, messaging, naming and coordination, without changing the kernels.
source: D1 of F5-44 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): introduction (goals, distribution transparency and its limits, t) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one node's current list of which nodes are in the cluster.
analogy: each friend's own list of who is "in" this week.
precise: in this course, the set of node ids a node believes alive, computed from messages received within a suspicion timeout and numbered so that changes are visible; different nodes may hold different views at the same moment.
source: D2 of F5-44 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (partial failure); R2 of F5-44 (three-node run: ssi_n1.log … ssi_n3.log, switch.log; QEMU 8.2.2 TCG; QEMU exit codes 33 (planned halts). Untested on hardware.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long a node waits without news before it removes another node from its view.
analogy: how many days without a letter before you stop counting a friend in.
precise: the time after the last message from a peer at which a heartbeat failure detector suspects the peer; it must be longer than the heartbeat period plus the expected delay, and every value trades detection speed against false suspicions.
source: D2 of F5-44 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (partial failure) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a process name that is unique in the whole cluster.
analogy: "Chidi's book number 7" instead of plain "book 7".
precise: a pair (node id, local process id), written node.pid in this course, so that process ids of different kernels never collide; a location-transparent system would hide the node part, ours deliberately shows it.
source: D1 of F5-44 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): introduction (goals, distribution transparency and its limits, t) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: running a program on another computer and getting its answer back.
analogy: asking a friend to do a sum for you and post the answer.
precise: placing a unit of work on a chosen node and returning its result to the requester, ideally with the same meaning as a local run; it inherits the failure ambiguity of remote procedure calls (F5-09).
source: D1 of F5-44 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): introduction (goals, distribution transparency and its limits, t) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a research operating system in which every resource on every machine is a file, reached with one protocol.
analogy: a town where every service, from books to printing, answers the same kinds of letter.
precise: a distributed operating system built at Bell Labs in which terminals, CPU servers and file servers share resources through the 9P file protocol, and each process assembles its own name space from local and remote file servers.
source: D1 of F5-45 (Rob Pike, Dave Presotto, Sean Dorward, Bob Flandrena, Ken Thompson, Howard Trickey, Phil Winterbottom, "Plan 9 from Bell Labs" (tier 2; journal and year to be r) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: Plan 9's small protocol for using files on another machine.
analogy: the library's six kinds of letter: find, open, read, write, stat, finished.
precise: a request–reply file protocol in which each T-message (request) is answered by an R-message (reply) or Rerror with the same tag; messages are size[4] type[1] tag[2] followed by type-specific fields, little-endian; 9P2000 is the classic revision, 9P2000.u and 9P2000.L are Unix and Linux extensions.
source: D3 of F5-45 (Plan 9 Programmer's Manual, section 5 (the 9P protocol: intro, version, attach, walk, open and create, read and write, clunk, flush, stat) (tier 1; edition to b); D9 of F5-45 (9P2000.u and 9P2000.L protocol descriptions published by the Linux v9fs implementers (tier 2; document and version to be recorded). Title only — not opened duri) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small number the client picks to stand for one file it is using on the server.
analogy: a numbered bookmark the library keeps for you.
precise: a 32-bit handle, chosen by the client, that the server associates with a file in the client's session from attach or walk until clunk; most 9P requests name a fid instead of a path.
source: D3 of F5-45 (Plan 9 Programmer's Manual, section 5 (the 9P protocol: intro, version, attach, walk, open and create, read and write, clunk, flush, stat) (tier 1; edition to b) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number that matches a reply to its request.
analogy: the reference number written on a letter and repeated on the answer.
precise: a 16-bit request identifier chosen by the client, unique among its outstanding requests and copied by the server into the reply, allowing many requests in flight on one connection; NOTAG (0xFFFF) is used only by Tversion.
source: D3 of F5-45 (Plan 9 Programmer's Manual, section 5 (the 9P protocol: intro, version, attach, walk, open and create, read and write, clunk, flush, stat) (tier 1; edition to b) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the server's unique identity for a file.
analogy: the library's own shelf number, which stays the same even if the book is renamed.
precise: a 13-byte value of type[1] (directory, append-only and other bits), version[4] (changes when the file changes) and path[8] (unique per file on that server); two files are the same file exactly when their qids' paths are equal.
source: D3 of F5-45 (Plan 9 Programmer's Manual, section 5 (the 9P protocol: intro, version, attach, walk, open and create, read and write, clunk, flush, stat) (tier 1; edition to b) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: each program has its own private map from path names to files.
analogy: each friend arranges their own shelf of borrowed books, from any library, in their own order.
precise: in Plan 9, a mount table per process (group) built with bind and mount, so that the same path can name different files in different processes; union directories let several directories appear at one path.
source: D2 of F5-45 (Rob Pike and co-authors, "The Use of Name Spaces in Plan 9" (tier 2; venue and year to be recorded). Title only — not opened during this build; the Source Resea) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a research distributed operating system in which programs run on a pool of processors and every resource is an object kept by some server.
analogy: a club where any free member does a job and every item has a sealed card instead of a member list.
precise: a distributed operating system from the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and CWI, built around a microkernel, a processor pool, RPC between clients and object servers, and capabilities for naming and protection.
source: D4 of F5-45 (Andrew S. Tanenbaum, Robbert van Renesse, Hans van Staveren, Gregory J. Sharp, Sape J. Mullender and co-authors, "Experiences with the Amoeba Distributed Operat) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an unforgeable ticket that names an object and says what its holder may do.
analogy: a tamper-proof club card that says "may read".
precise: a bit string containing a server port, an object number, a rights field and a check field derived from a server-held secret with a one-way function, so that holders can pass it on but cannot raise its rights or guess a valid one; "sparse" because valid values are a tiny fraction of the possible ones.
source: D5 of F5-45 (Andrew S. Tanenbaum, Sape J. Mullender, Robbert van Renesse, "Using Sparse Capabilities in a Distributed Operating System" (tier 2; venue and year to be recorde) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a set of computers with no owner that the system hands out for running programs.
analogy: whichever friend is free does the next job.
precise: in Amoeba, processors not attached to users' terminals, allocated to processes by the system at run time, so that the user's view is of one large computer rather than of personal machines.
source: D4 of F5-45 (Andrew S. Tanenbaum, Robbert van Renesse, Hans van Staveren, Gregory J. Sharp, Sape J. Mullender and co-authors, "Experiences with the Amoeba Distributed Operat) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the shared memory rings through which a virtual device and its driver pass buffers.
analogy: an in-tray and an out-tray between you and the library clerk.
precise: a descriptor table, an available ring written by the driver and a used ring written by the device, in guest memory; the driver queues chains of descriptors and notifies the device, the device returns finished chains with the number of bytes it wrote.
source: D7 of F5-45 (OASIS, "Virtual I/O Device (VIRTIO) Specification" (tier 1; version to be recorded): legacy interface over PCI, split virtqueues, the 9P transport device. Title) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: starting a computer with a program it loads over the network instead of from its own disk.
analogy: the new friend is posted the club's rulebook.
precise: a boot in which firmware on the network card (PXE, or a replacement such as iPXE) obtains an address and the name of a boot file by DHCP, downloads the file by TFTP (or another protocol), and runs it.
source: D1 of F5-46 (Intel, "Preboot Execution Environment (PXE) Specification" (tier 1; version to be recorded). Title only — not opened during this build; the Source Researcher mu) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a very small protocol for downloading a file, one block at a time.
analogy: the rulebook sent in numbered envelopes, each acknowledged before the next.
precise: the Trivial File Transfer Protocol over UDP: a read request names the file; the server sends numbered data blocks, each acknowledged before the next (lock-step); a block shorter than the block size ends the transfer; options such as block size and transfer size can be negotiated.
source: D3 of F5-46 (The TFTP specification ("The TFTP Protocol (Revision 2)") and its option extensions for block size and transfer size (IETF RFCs; numbers to be recorded by the S) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: open-source network boot firmware that can run small boot scripts.
analogy: a helpful neighbour who fetches the rulebook and hands it over.
precise: a network boot program, shipped as option ROMs with QEMU, that performs DHCP, fetches files by TFTP and other protocols, runs scripts that start with #!ipxe, and can load Multiboot kernels with a command line.
source: D4 of F5-46 (iPXE project documentation (tier 2): scripting (#!ipxe, kernel, boot), Multiboot support, image verification. Title only — not opened during this build; the scr) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the name of the first file a network-booting machine should fetch.
analogy: "ask for n4.ipxe".
precise: the file name a DHCP server gives a client (the "file" field or a boot-file-name option), interpreted relative to the TFTP server.
source: D2 of F5-46 (IETF RFC 2131, "Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol", and the DHCP options RFC (number to be recorded) (tier 1). Title only — not opened during this build (doss) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: files kept on one machine and used from others as if they were local.
analogy: the club notebook at Amara's house, written by letter.
precise: a file service in which clients send file operations to a server by RPC; its design is described by its naming, its state (stateful or stateless server), its caching and the consistency guarantees it gives to concurrent clients.
source: D7 of F5-46 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): distributed file systems (NFS, stateful and stateless servers, c) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a copy of file data kept on the client to save trips to the server.
analogy: a photocopy of a notebook page.
precise: client-side storage of file data or attributes, used instead of a server request; its correctness depends on when the client checks that the copy is still current (revalidation) or on the server telling the client when it is not (callbacks, leases).
source: D7 of F5-46 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): distributed file systems (NFS, stateful and stateless servers, c) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: asking the server whether your copy is still the newest before you use it.
analogy: phoning the library: "is page 3 still edition 2?"
precise: a small request (here a stat) that returns the file's current version, compared with the cached version; on a match the cache is used, otherwise the data is fetched again. It costs one round trip per use and fails when the server is unreachable.
source: D7 of F5-46 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): distributed file systems (NFS, stateful and stateless servers, c) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: after one client closes a file it changed, any client that opens the file afterwards sees the change.
analogy: once Bao has posted his page back, anyone who borrows the notebook next sees his writing.
precise: a weaker guarantee than one-copy (UNIX) semantics in which writes are flushed on close and caches are revalidated on open; concurrent readers and writers of an open file may see different data.
source: D7 of F5-46 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): distributed file systems (NFS, stateful and stateless servers, c); D10 of F5-46 (John H. Howard and co-authors, "Scale and Performance in a Distributed File System" (AFS) (tier 2; venue and year to be recorded); Russel Sandberg and co-author) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a server that remembers what each client is doing.
analogy: Amara remembers which friend has which bookmark.
precise: a server that keeps per-client state between requests (open files, fids, locks, cache promises); it allows short requests and server-driven cache invalidation, but its state is lost when it crashes and must be rebuilt or invalidated, and clients that crash leave state behind.
source: D7 of F5-46 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): distributed file systems (NFS, stateful and stateless servers, c) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the shared services that make many machines act as one cluster: who is in, what is agreed, what runs where.
analogy: the club's list of members, its notebook of decisions, and its organiser.
precise: in this course, membership (F5-44), a consensus-replicated state machine holding locks and the job table, and a scheduler driven by that state machine, running in every node's kernel.
source: G1 of F5-47 (University Authoring Guide (this project), section 11.6 (MP2, quoted), section 11.4 (exams), section 11.2 (forensic rubric), section 5 course card DS403. A map,) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the position of a command in the shared list of commands.
analogy: the line number in the club notebook.
precise: a position, counted from 1, in the log that Raft replicates; an entry is identified by its index and the term in which a leader created it, and two logs that hold an entry with the same index and term are identical up to that index.
source: D1 of F5-47 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm" (the Raft paper; extended version) (tier 2). Title only — not opened during ) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a follower throwing away entries that the leader does not have.
analogy: crossing out lines you wrote in your copy of the notebook while you could not reach the friend who keeps the real one.
precise: when an append from the current leader carries an entry whose term differs from the follower's entry at the same index, the follower deletes that entry and all after it; only uncommitted entries can be deleted this way.
source: D1 of F5-47 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm" (the Raft paper; extended version) (tier 2). Title only — not opened during ) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the honest answer when a request timed out: it may or may not have happened.
analogy: "I posted the letter; I never heard back."
precise: the result a client must report when it received no commit confirmation in time; the command may later be committed (by this or a later leader) or discarded, so the client must not assume either and must check or retry idempotently.
source: D2 of F5-47 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): leaders and the truth defined by the majority, fencing tokens, linea) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part that decides which node runs each job, with its decisions written in the shared log.
analogy: the organiser assigning chores, writing each assignment in the notebook.
precise: a leader-side loop that proposes JOB_ASSIGN entries for submitted jobs and for jobs whose node left the view; workers start a job only when the assignment is applied, and report completion through the log, so that every node agrees on each job's state.
source: D3 of F5-47 (Abhishek Verma and co-authors, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg" (tier 2; venue and year to be recorded). Title only — not opened during this) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "whoever has the lowest number among the nodes I can see is in charge."
analogy: "the friend with the oldest membership card who answers the phone decides."
precise: a leader-selection rule computed from each node's own membership view, with no majority requirement; under a partition every side elects a leader and accepts writes.
source: R4 of F5-47 (naive (split-brain) run: splitbrain_n1.log … splitbrain_n3.log, splitbrain_switch.log, splitbrain_check.log (result: expected-fail).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a meeting where engineers examine a design before (or while) it is built, looking for what can go wrong.
analogy: the club reading the new rules aloud and asking "what if the phones are down?"
precise: a structured review of a written design against requirements and failure scenarios, with named reviewers, recorded findings and a decision; in this university, the R1–R4 gates of mega projects and the P exam of DS403.
source: G1 of F5-47 (University Authoring Guide (this project), section 11.6 (MP2, quoted), section 11.4 (exams), section 11.2 (forensic rubric), section 5 course card DS403. A map,) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
